donor_lane.method: Verified via git ls-remote (HEAD sha) + blobless depth-1 no-checkout clones (git clone --filter=blob:none --depth 1 --no-checkout). Paths via `git ls-tree -r --name-only HEAD` (free, local, no blob fetch). Full-repo `git ls-tree -r -l HEAD` (blob sizes) triggers a per-blob network fetch (~0.3-0.5s/object even with GitHub's own smart-HTTP negotiation via the proxy) which is only tractable for small repos. For repos with >1000 tracked files, total 'source bytes' is an ESTIMATE: an even-stride sample of ~150-220 paths was sized with `ls-tree -l`, averaged, and extrapolated by file count, after excluding obvious non-source outliers (locale .po files, chart-of-accounts JSON fixtures, generated docs sites, placeholder images/icons) that otherwise skew a small sample heavily. These are marked total_bytes_estimated=true. Mechanism-slice byte counts are always EXACT (targeted ls-tree -l on a short, named file list). Every clone was deleted immediately after use; peak per-repo disk footprint stayed under ~10MB.

candidates.name: OpenSCAD
candidates.license_spdx: GPL-2.0-or-later WITH CGAL-linking-exception (COPYING = GPLv2 text plus an explicit permission to link with CGAL and distribute the result)
candidates.notes: Dual backend: legacy CGAL Nef-polyhedron boolean ops (src/geometry/cgal/*) and a newer Manifold-library backend (src/geometry/manifold/*). GeometryEvaluator walks the AbstractNode tree and dispatches per-node-type geometry generation; CSGTreeEvaluator builds a flattened CSG op tree consumed by the render/preview path. export_stl.cc writes ASCII or binary STL directly off a PolySet (triangulated mesh).

mechanism_slice.description: CSG tree construction/evaluation + geometry evaluator + STL export/import

candidates.name: CadQuery
candidates.notes: cq.py implements the fluent Workplane API (chained parametric ops: box/extrude/fillet/pattern etc.) as a stack machine over occ_impl.shapes.Shape, a thin OCCT/OCP wrapper. assembly.py + occ_impl/assembly.py handle multi-part Assembly trees with placement constraints. occ_impl/exporters/ dispatches STL/STEP/AMF/3MF/SVG/DXF export from the underlying OCCT BRep. This is the highest-fidelity 'parametric geometry kernel with a scriptable Python API' donor candidate — smallest, cleanest, most directly reusable slice of the whole set.

mechanism_slice.description: Workplane/parametric fluent API, Assembly, OCC-backed shapes, and exporters

candidates.name: FreeCAD
candidates.license_spdx: LGPL-2.1-or-later (LICENSE file; individual workbenches/modules carry mixed GPL-2.0/GPL-3.0/LGPL notices)
candidates.notes: No mechanism slice requested for FreeCAD in scope; included only for URL/sha/license/size comparison. Far larger and heavier (full parametric-history CAD kernel + GUI + many workbenches) than CadQuery for a scripted parametric-geometry absorption.

candidates.name: OCCT (Open CASCADE Technology)
candidates.notes: The C++ B-Rep kernel CadQuery itself wraps (via OCP/pythonocc bindings). No mechanism slice requested; included for comparison only. Absorbing OCCT directly (vs. via CadQuery's Python layer) would be a much heavier lift.

candidates.name: KiCad
candidates.license_spdx: GPL-3.0-or-later (main LICENSE; bundled third-party bits under LICENSE.3-CLAUSE-BSD/APACHE-2.0/BOOSTv1_0/CC-BY-SA-4.0/CC0/ISC/MIT per LICENSE.README)
candidates.notes: BOM: eeschema/bom_plugins.cpp + dialog_bom.cpp drive pluggable BOM generators (Python scripts under eeschema/python_scripts/*.py, e.g. bom_csv_grouped_by_value.py) fed by common/jobs/job_export_bom.cpp for CLI use. Netlist: netlist_reader/netlist.cpp holds the in-memory component/net graph; per-target exporters (KiCad/Spice/Cadstar/Allegro/PADS/OrcadPCB2) subclass netlist_exporter_base.cpp. ERC (schematic rule check) and DRC (board rule check, pcbnew/drc/drc_engine.cpp + drc_rule.cpp, a declarative rule-condition parser) are two separate engines, not shared, each with their own item/report/exclusion model.

mechanism_slice.description: BOM generation, netlist graph construction/export, ERC and DRC rule model entry points

candidates.name: CuraEngine
candidates.notes: TimeEstimateCalculator (timeEstimate.h/.cpp) is explicitly commented in-source as 'adapted from the Marlin sources': a per-move Block with accelerate_until/decelerate_after/nominal_feedrate/entry_speed/max_entry_speed plus per-axis jerk limits (max_xy_jerk, max_z_jerk, max_e_jerk) -- i.e. a full trapezoidal-velocity-profile planner simulation per G-code move, not a flat feedrate/distance division. TimeMaterialEstimates.h carries the per-feature-type (wall/skin/infill/travel/retraction) time+material rollup that LayerPlan/GCodeExport accumulate into. slicer.cpp/slicer.h is the actual mesh-to-layers slicing entry point (SlicerLayer per Z height), independent of and upstream from the time estimator.

mechanism_slice.description: Print time estimation (TimeEstimateCalculator, Marlin-derived), layer slicing entry point, per-move time/material estimate struct

candidates.name: PrusaSlicer
candidates.notes: IMPORTANT: this HEAD is a heavily modularized/refactored PrusaSlicer tree (src/libpgcode, src/slic3r-domain, src/slic3r-biz-* modules) very different from the classic monolithic 'src/libslic3r/GCode/GCodeProcessor.*' layout most public docs describe -- confirms this is genuinely live upstream, not a stale mirror. TimeBlock.{hpp,cpp} implements the identical physical model to CuraEngine (per-move Trapezoid: accelerate_until/decelerate_after/cruise_feedrate, closed-form kinematics: v^2=v0^2+2ad style formulas, entry/exit feedrate handed in per block) -- both slicers converged on the same Marlin-derived per-segment trapezoidal-acceleration time model, just organized differently. PrintStatistics.hpp (src/slic3r-domain) is the material/filament usage output: used_filament_per_extruder_{mm,cm3,g}, filament_cost_per_extruder, volumes_per_extruder/per_role, wipe-tower and flush volumes -- i.e. cost and mass, not just length.

mechanism_slice.description: Print time estimation (TimeBlock/TimeProcessor, same trapezoidal-planner family as CuraEngine but modularized into a standalone libpgcode library), slicing entry point (Print.cpp, TriangleMeshSlicer), filament/material usage stats

candidates.name: ERPNext
candidates.notes: This HEAD has already extracted BOM cost logic out of the historical monolithic bom.py into erpnext/manufacturing/doctype/bom/services/costing.py (BOMCostingService) + exploded_items.py (BOMExplodedItemsService); bom.py now keeps thin delegating stubs. Key formula (BOMCostingService.calculate_cost): total_cost = operating_cost + raw_material_cost - secondary_items_cost, with base_total_cost mirroring it in company currency. calculate_op_cost sums operation.operating_cost = hour_rate * time_in_mins/60 (or a flat fg_based_operating_cost = quantity * operating_cost_per_bom_quantity). calculate_rm_cost sums rate*qty over BOM items using get_rm_rate (valuation-rate / price-list / sub-assembly-BOM-unit-cost, selectable per BOM). calculate_secondary_items_costs replaces the old 'Scrap Items' concept: rows valued 'Valuation Rate' or 'Manual' are summed and subtracted first, and the remainder (raw_material_cost - own-valued secondary cost) is allocated pro-rata by cost_allocation_per % across the remaining secondary rows -- i.e. scrap/byproduct cost is netted OUT of raw_material_cost, not added. calculate_exploded_cost then re-rates the flattened BOM Explosion Item rows (get_rm_rate_map, walking child sub-assembly BOMs) so the exploded (fully-flattened) BOM view reprices consistently. work_order.py + services/required_items.py compute required raw-material quantities off qty_consumed_per_unit, and services/reservation.py handles stock reservation against a Work Order.

mechanism_slice.description: BOM doctype (cost rollup, exploded-items, operations cost) and Work Order

candidates.name: Medusa
candidates.license_spdx: MIT (core repository; a separate Enterprise Edition subset is under a proprietary commercial license per ENTERPRISE-LICENSE.md, not applicable to the modules examined here)
candidates.notes: Medusa v2's modular architecture deliberately does NOT put price_set_id or inventory_item_id foreign keys on ProductVariant. Instead each module (Product, Pricing, Inventory) is a standalone, independently-schema'd package, and a separate 'link module' (packages/modules/link-modules) owns join tables: product_variant_price_set (pvps) and product_variant_inventory_item (pvitem, with its own extra field required_quantity for multi-part variants). These link definitions also declare computed field aliases back onto ProductVariant (e.g. variant.calculated_price resolves through price_set_link.price_set.calculated_price; variant.inventory resolves through inventory_items.inventory) so the cross-module join is transparent to API consumers via Medusa's remote-query layer. Price itself (models/price.ts) is currency_code + amount + min/max_quantity (quantity-tier pricing) belonging to a PriceSet, with PriceRule rows layered on for conditional pricing (e.g. by region/customer-group) and PriceList for list-based overrides -- i.e. price is NOT a flat variant.price column, it's a rule-evaluated PriceSet resolved at query time.

mechanism_slice.description: Product/variant module, Pricing module (PriceSet/Price/PriceRule/PriceList), Inventory module, and the cross-module link definitions that connect them

candidates.name: Saleor
candidates.notes: Classic normalized Django relational model, the opposite architectural pole from Medusa: warehouse/models.py's Stock has direct ForeignKeys product_variant and warehouse plus integer quantity/quantity_allocated columns; Allocation FKs an order_line to a Stock with quantity_allocated, and AllocationQueryset.annotate_stock_available_quantity computes available = stock.quantity - sum(allocations.quantity_allocated) via a DB aggregate. No separate link-module indirection -- stock and variant are directly joined tables in one schema.

mechanism_slice.description: Product/variant models, Warehouse/Stock models, Discount (pricing rule) models

cross_repo_readouts.prusaslicer_time_model: Per-move trapezoidal velocity profile (accelerate/cruise/decelerate segments) with closed-form kinematics (v^2 = v0^2 + 2*a*s), computed per TimeBlock (one per G1 move), with entry/exit feedrate continuity across the move sequence (junction speeds). Key functions: Trapezoid::acceleration_time/deceleration_time/cruise_time, TimeBlock::calculate_trapezoid, TimeBlock::time().
cross_repo_readouts.curaengine_time_model: Same physical model, explicitly derived from Marlin firmware's stepper planner: TimeEstimateCalculator::Block with accelerate_until/decelerate_after/nominal_feedrate/entry_speed/max_entry_speed and per-axis jerk limits. Both slicers therefore model print time as a chain of trapezoidal-acceleration segments, not a flat distance/feedrate division -- meaningfully more accurate than 'volume / average flow rate' style estimates, and the two independent codebases corroborating the same model gives confidence it's the right level of physical fidelity to absorb.
cross_repo_readouts.erpnext_bom_cost_rollup: total_cost = operating_cost + raw_material_cost - secondary_items_cost (BOMCostingService.calculate_cost, erpnext/manufacturing/doctype/bom/services/costing.py). raw_material_cost = sum(rate * qty) over BOM items, rate from valuation-rate/price-list/sub-assembly-unit-cost (calculate_rm_cost/get_rm_rate). operating_cost = sum(hour_rate * time_in_mins/60) per operation, or quantity * operating_cost_per_bom_quantity flat (calculate_op_cost). secondary_items_cost (the modern rename of 'scrap items') nets byproduct/scrap value OUT: rows valued directly (Valuation Rate/Manual) are summed first, the remainder of raw_material_cost is allocated pro-rata by % across the rest (calculate_secondary_items_costs / _set_own_cost_secondary_items). calculate_exploded_cost then re-rates the fully flattened (exploded) BOM tree by walking child sub-assembly BOMs via get_rm_rate_map.
cross_repo_readouts.medusa_variant_price_inventory_link: ProductVariant carries no price or inventory FK. Cross-module 'link' tables (product_variant_price_set, product_variant_inventory_item) owned by packages/modules/link-modules join Product<->Pricing and Product<->Inventory, each with declared field aliases so variant.calculated_price / variant.inventory resolve transitively at query time through the link. Price rows are currency_code + amount + min/max_quantity under a PriceSet, with PriceRule for conditional (region/customer-group) pricing and PriceList for list overrides -- price is rule-resolved, not a flat column.

recommendation.highest_leverage_first_absorption: CadQuery's workplane/parametric-geometry-and-export stack (cadquery/cq.py + occ_impl/shapes.py + occ_impl/exporters), paired with CuraEngine's or PrusaSlicer's TimeBlock/TimeEstimateCalculator print-time model, feeding ERPNext's BOM cost-rollup formula.
recommendation.reasoning: The milestone is: product hypothesis -> parametric geometry -> material/print estimate -> BOM -> unit economics -> SKU. That chain has a natural bottleneck and it is geometry-to-time-estimate, not any single donor in isolation. CadQuery is the cheapest, cleanest entry point for 'parametric geometry' because it is pure Python (12MB total, MIT-compatible Apache-2.0 license, no GUI to strip, no CGAL/OCCT-exception licensing wrinkle to reason about) and its Workplane API already returns a manifold BRep/mesh plus a working STL/3MF/STEP exporter -- i.e. it is a scriptable geometry kernel we can drive headlessly from a product-hypothesis parameter set with no UI absorption cost. OpenSCAD is a close second (also small) but its CSG-tree evaluator is coupled to a bespoke declarative language (.scad) and a dual CGAL/Manifold backend that adds absorption surface area for no corresponding product benefit if the goal is a parametric Python pipeline. FreeCAD and OCCT are both an order of magnitude to two orders of magnitude larger and mostly GUI/workbench weight we would not use. For material/print estimate, CuraEngine and PrusaSlicer converge independently on the same physical model (trapezoidal per-move acceleration time + per-role filament volume/weight/cost), which is the right fidelity for a real print-time and material-cost number per SKU; CuraEngine is the smaller, more self-contained codebase to lift the TimeEstimateCalculator out of (653 files, 8.2MB total vs. PrusaSlicer's much larger and more entangled slicing pipeline), though PrusaSlicer's PrintStatistics gives a cleaner already-separated cost/weight-per-extruder output shape to mirror. ERPNext's BOM cost-rollup formula (operating_cost + raw_material_cost - secondary_items_cost, with pro-rata scrap/byproduct netting and sub-assembly-aware exploded-cost re-rating) is a compact, already-battle-tested unit-economics formula we can reimplement natively in a few hundred lines rather than adopt wholesale -- ERPNext's own repo is a full Frappe framework app (5600+ files) we do not want to run just to get one costing formula. Medusa's and Saleor's product/variant/price/inventory models matter for the final 'SKU' step, but that is the last link in the chain and both are viable (Medusa if we want multi-currency/rule-based pricing and decoupled inventory later; Saleor if we want a simpler directly-joined relational model sooner) -- neither is the bottleneck, so neither should be the FIRST absorption. In short: CadQuery-style parametric geometry -> CuraEngine/PrusaSlicer-style trapezoidal time+material estimate is the one dependency edge that nothing else in Atlas can currently produce, and it directly unblocks 'material/print estimate' and therefore the BOM and unit-economics steps behind it; the commerce-side (BOM ledger math, SKU/variant/price modeling) can be built or absorbed afterward with much lower risk since ERPNext/Medusa/Saleor's relevant slices are all small, well-isolated formulas/models rather than deep physical or geometric subsystems.
